description:
You are a housing policy analyst at the San Francisco Planning Department. The Mayor's office has requested a data-driven Displacement Risk Index (DRI) to guide the allocation of the city's anti-displacement investment fund across census tracts.

Residential displacement risk is driven by three independent pressures that must all be reflected in your index: (1) household vulnerability — the concentration of low-income residents in a zone who cannot afford to move elsewhere; (2) housing precarity — the age and quality of the existing building stock, since older buildings in poor condition are prime candidates for demolition-rebuild speculation; and (3) development pressure — how close existing buildings are to the maximum density allowed by zoning, indicating speculator interest.

Using the San Francisco UrbanSim dataset at /home/ga/urbansim_projects/data/sanfran_public.h5, build a Displacement Risk Index for every zone that has both residential households and buildings. Combine all three components into a final DRI score. The methodology — including how you define low-income, how you measure housing precarity, how you weight the components, and how you normalize — is entirely your decision as the analyst.

Deliver:
- /home/ga/urbansim_projects/output/displacement_risk.csv — one row per zone, with columns: zone_id, dri_score, vulnerability_score, precarity_score, pressure_score, low_income_households, total_households, mean_price_per_sqft
- /home/ga/urbansim_projects/output/displacement_risk_chart.png — horizontal bar chart of the 20 highest-DRI zones, sorted descending

The analysis must be done in a Jupyter notebook at /home/ga/urbansim_projects/notebooks/displacement_risk.ipynb using the UrbanSim (Python 3) kernel. Jupyter Lab is open in Firefox at http://localhost:8888.
